summary: The cover letter is a narrative artifact — a focused, one-page argument for why this human should be in this role at this company. Customization per application is non-negotiable.

facts.text: The cover letter is a narrative artifact - a focused, one-page argument for why this human should be in this role at this company. Customization per application is non-negotiable.
Why this company. Show evidence you've done your homework: a product they shipped, a value they've published.
Why this role. Connect the specific responsibilities to specific skills or experiences you have. Reuse 2-3 keywords from the JD.
Why me. Demonstrate through evidence and stories. Don't list skills; show outcomes.
"I am writing to apply for the X position at Y."
"My name is X and I am a [degree/title]."
Stronger openers:
"I noticed your team published the design for the X system last month - the tradeoffs you made on Y are the same ones I worked through at Z."
Weak: "I have strong project management skills and am highly organized."
Stronger: "Last year I shipped the X migration on a six-engineer team. The original estimate was four months; we delivered in five because I caught a dependency that wasn't in the original scope."
One page maximum, no exceptions.
250-350 words is the standard target.
3-4 short paragraphs, block-formatted.
At a minimum, customize:
Company name and the "why this company" paragraph
2-3 keywords from the JD
The job title in the opener
Salutation: "Dear [Name]," when you know the hiring manager's name.
Sign-off: "Sincerely," is the universal safe choice.
Capitalization: Only the first word of the closing phrase is capitalized.
Count how many sentences open with "I." If more than half do, the letter reads self-absorbed. Vary openings: lead with the company, the role, the project, the result.
The cliché opener. "I am writing to apply..."
The reused letter. Generic flattery, no company name in the first paragraph.
The skill list. "Strong communicator, fast learner, team player."
The resume rehash. Repeating the resume's bullets in paragraph form.
The two-page letter. Always cut to one page.
The typo in the company name. Auto-disqualifying.
Ask a Manager - this is how to write a good cover letter (Alison Green, 2024)
Harvard Business Review - Cover Letters Still Matter (2025)
Applying to a role where the job posting invites a cover letter, or where a hiring manager's stated preferences signal one will actually be read.
